secondaryCondition: Cholelithiasis (chronic gallstone disease, predominantly pigment stones) complicating service-connected cirrhosis of the liver
secondaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.114, DC 7315 (cholelithiasis, chronic) — evaluated by reference to DC 7314 (chronic biliary tract disease): 30 percent with three or more clinically documented attacks of right-upper-quadrant pain with nausea and vomiting in the past 12 months or requiring biliary stricture dilatation at least once in the past 12 months; 10 percent with one or two such documented attacks; 0 percent if asymptomatic with no documented attack in the past 12 months. Qualified-human rating review required; where stones are asymptomatic the schedule yields 0 percent, and where cholecystectomy complications dominate, DC 7318 applies instead
primaryCondition: Service-connected cirrhosis of the liver (hepatic cirrhosis) with documented hepatic synthetic dysfunction or portal hypertension
primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.114, DC 7312 (cirrhosis of the liver), assigned on Model for End-Stage Liver Disease score or on continuous daily debilitating symptoms with ascites, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, hepatic encephalopathy, variceal hemorrhage, coagulopathy, portal gastropathy, or hepatopulmonary/hepatorenal syndrome, with Note (3) allowing rating on symptomatology where no Model for End-Stage Liver Disease score exists in the record
etiologicalMechanism: Bile-composition and gallbladder-motility sequence: in service-connected cirrhosis of the liver, three convergent derangements shift bile from cholesterol-saturated toward pigment-stone lithogenicity. First, hepatocyte dysfunction reduces bile-salt synthesis and canalicular bile-salt secretion, lowering the bile-salt pool and with it the capacity to keep cholesterol and unconjugated bilirubin in micellar solution. Second, portal hypertension with hypersplenism accelerates erythrocyte sequestration and turnover, while impaired hepatic glucuronidation reduces conjugation of bilirubin, so the biliary load of unconjugated, water-insoluble pigment rises. Third, gallbladder motor function is impaired in cirrhosis — reduced cholecystokinin responsiveness, gallbladder wall thickening, and elevated circulating estrogens from reduced hepatic clearance all promote stasis and crystal nucleation; the resulting stones in cirrhosis are most often pigment stones and are frequently asymptomatic. Del Olmo et al. (PMID 9361181), a controlled cohort of 313 histologically or laparoscopically confirmed cirrhosis patients against 357 liver-disease-free comparison patients, reported higher prevalence and incidence of gallstone disease in cirrhosis and concluded that cirrhosis of the liver may be considered a risk factor for cholecystolithiasis. Mallick and Anand (PMID 35535063) review the pathogenesis and management of gallstone disease in cirrhosis, reporting a prevalence of gallstone disease in cirrhosis of roughly 25 to 30 percent, substantially above general-population estimates, and attributing it to the altered bile composition and gallbladder dysmotility described above. Wang et al. (PMID 38382725), a systematic review and meta-analysis pooling 115 studies and more than 32 million participants, place pooled global gallstone prevalence at approximately 6.1 percent, which supplies the population-level comparator against which the cirrhosis-specific prevalence is contrasted. Framing under 38 CFR § 3.310: this is a § 3.310(a) direct-causation theory — the service-connected cirrhosis is asserted to have produced a new pathological entity, symptomatic chronic cholelithiasis, rather than merely to have worsened a baseline lithogenic tendency. A § 3.310(b) aggravation theory is not the theory offered here, because the literature describes stone formation in a previously stone-free biliary tree rather than measurable worsening of documented pre-existing stones; if the record shows gallstones documented before the cirrhosis-associated derangement, the case must be re-pleaded as aggravation of a baseline condition in which the cirrhosis-attributable increment is separated from the natural progression of age- and obesity-related stone disease, and § 3.310(b) then governs. Chronology is decisive: the corresponding § 3.310(a) and § 3.310(b) analysis requires imaging evidence of cholecystolithiasis after the clinical onset of cirrhosis, together with the cirrhosis diagnosis itself, so that the nexus opinion can state that the gallstone disease is at least as likely as not causally related to the service-connected cirrhosis — a conclusion that requires documented chronology, accounted-for competing causes, and an approximate balance of evidence, consistent with § 3.102 and with the requirement that the opinion rest on evidence of record rather than on speculation. Competing causes that must be excluded or weighed include advancing age, female sex, obesity and metabolic syndrome, rapid weight loss or bariatric surgery, pregnancy, hemolytic disorders independent of portal hypertension, hepatitis C infection and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease as separate hepatic drivers within the same liver, ileal disease or resection, prolonged fasting or total parenteral nutrition, and fibrate or somatostatin-analog medication, as well as genetic lithogenic predisposition; none of these operates to defeat the theory, but each must be addressed in the individual case because population-level relative risks do not transfer to the individual claimant. No individual probability is asserted here. Rating caution under § 4.14: cholelithiasis symptoms may be rated only once, and where the same abdominal pain, nausea, or vomiting supports an evaluation of the cirrhosis or of a residual gastropathy, the rating schedule's own anti-pyramiding instruction for DCs 7301 through 7329 requires a single evaluation under the diagnostic code reflecting the predominant disability picture, so § 4.14 bars duplicative compensation for the same manifestations.

medicalEvidence.title: Prevalence and incidence of gallstones in liver cirrhosis
medicalEvidence.authors: J A Del Olmo; F García; M A Serra; L Maldonado; J M Rodrigo
medicalEvidence.summary: Controlled study of 313 patients with cirrhosis confirmed by histology and/or laparoscopy and 357 liver-disease-free comparison patients undergoing ultrasonographic examination: prevalence and incidence of gallstone disease were higher in cirrhosis, and the authors concluded that cirrhosis of the liver may be considered a risk factor for cholecystolithiasis — the primary human evidence that cirrhosis precedes and predicts gallstone formation.

medicalEvidence.title: Gallstone Disease in Cirrhosis-Pathogenesis and Management
medicalEvidence.summary: Review reporting that gallstones are more common in patients with cirrhosis and that incidence rises with severity of liver disease, that pigment stones predominate in cirrhosis and usually remain asymptomatic, and that the mechanism involves altered bile composition and gallbladder dysmotility — the mechanistic source for the lithogenic pathway asserted in this row.

medicalEvidence.title: Global Epidemiology of Gallstones in the 21st Century: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
medicalEvidence.authors: Xin Wang; Wenqian Yu; Guoheng Jiang; Hongyu Li; Shiyi Li; Linjun Xie; Xuan Bai; Ping Cui; Qi Chen; Yanmei Lou; Li Zou; Sulian Li; Zhongfang Zhou; Chi Zhang; Peng Sun; Min Mao
medicalEvidence.summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 115 studies and more than 32 million participants estimating pooled global gallstone prevalence at approximately 6.1 percent with geographic and sex variation — the general-population denominator against which the higher cirrhosis-specific prevalence is compared.

secondaryCondition: Fibromyalgia (primary fibromyalgia syndrome with widespread musculoskeletal pain) in a veteran with service-connected hypothyroidism
secondaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.71a, DC 5025 (fibromyalgia (fibrositis, primary fibromyalgia syndrome)): 40 percent for widespread musculoskeletal pain and tender points that are constant or nearly so and refractory to therapy; 20 percent for episodic pain present more than one-third of the time, often precipitated by environmental or emotional stress or overexertion; 10 percent when continuous medication is required for control. Note to DC 5025 defines widespread pain as pain on both sides of the body, above and below the waist, affecting both the axial skeleton and the extremities. Qualified-human rating review required
primaryCondition: Service-connected hypothyroidism, biochemically documented by elevated thyroid-stimulating hormone with low or low-normal free thyroxine
primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.119, DC 7903 (hypothyroidism): 100 percent for hypothyroidism manifesting as myxedema; 30 percent for hypothyroidism without myxedema; with Notes (1) and (2) directing that after the initial diagnostic period the residual effects of hypothyroidism be rated under the appropriate diagnostic codes within the appropriate body systems
etiologicalMechanism: Endocrine-myopathic and central-sensitization sequence: thyroid hormone deficiency slows skeletal-muscle relaxation and mitochondrial oxidative metabolism, producing a hypothyroid myopathy with aching, stiffness, cramps, and exercise intolerance, and it alters peripheral and central nociceptive processing so that a chronic widespread-pain phenotype can emerge. In parallel, the autoimmune thyroiditis that is the leading cause of hypothyroidism in the United States shares inflammatory and neuroimmune pathways with fibromyalgia, so affected individuals can carry both the endocrine deficiency and a centrally amplified pain state. Haliloglu et al. (PMID 28176037) examined fibromyalgia in patients with thyroid autoimmunity and reported a fibromyalgia prevalence of approximately 30 to 40 percent in Hashimoto thyroiditis with structural pathology against roughly 2 to 7 percent in the general population, alongside a relationship with disease activity. Park et al. (PMID 34369360) performed a systematic review and meta-analysis of the relationship between fibromyalgia and thyroid autoimmunity, finding an association with widespread chronic pain together with correlated clinical symptoms and depression. Nishioka et al. (PMID 27905199) measured thyroid autoantibodies in 207 patients with clinically defined fibromyalgia syndrome and found a high prevalence of anti-thyroid-stimulating-hormone-receptor antibody, indicating a substantial autoimmune-thyroid overlap population. Framing under 38 CFR § 3.310: this is a § 3.310(a) direct-causation theory, in which the service-connected hypothyroidism is asserted to have produced a new and separately diagnosable condition, fibromyalgia, with its own rating criteria under DC 5025. It is not offered as a § 3.310(b) aggravation theory; an aggravation theory would be required only where the record documents fibromyalgia predating the hypothyroidism and the claim is that the endocrine disease measurably worsened a pre-existing baseline pain disorder, in which case the hypothyroidism-attributable increment must be separated from the natural progression of the pre-existing fibromyalgia and § 3.310(b) governs. Chronology and the individual analysis under § 3.310(a)/(b) require the hypothyroidism diagnosis and its laboratory confirmation to precede or coincide with the fibromyalgia diagnosis, so that the clinician can state that the fibromyalgia is at least as likely as not caused by the service-connected hypothyroidism — an opinion that must rest on a documented temporal sequence, a rule-out of competing causes, and an approximate balance of evidence consistent with § 3.102, and not on the population associations cited here. Competing causes that must be weighed include primary sleep disturbance and obstructive sleep apnea, major depressive and anxiety disorders, physical deconditioning after injury, other autoimmune disease such as rheumatoid arthritis or Sjögren's syndrome, statin and other medication-related myalgia, vitamin D deficiency, hepatitis C, and small-fiber neuropathy, all of which can independently produce widespread pain and fatigue. Reporting caution is required in the individual case: the cited studies define their populations by thyroid autoimmunity rather than by biochemically confirmed hypothyroidism alone, so a nexus opinion must document hypothyroidism by laboratory testing and must not treat the autoimmune-thyroid association as proof that hypothyroidism itself caused the pain. No individual probability is asserted here. Rating discipline under § 4.14: fibromyalgia fatigue, sleep disturbance, and depression may not be compensated twice, and where the same manifestations support a mental-disorder evaluation under § 4.130, the higher single evaluation principle applies so that § 4.14 bars duplicative ratings for one symptom picture.

medicalEvidence.title: Fibromyalgia in patients with thyroid autoimmunity: prevalence and relationship with disease activity
medicalEvidence.authors: Sema Haliloglu; Bilge Ekinci; Hulya Uzkeser; Hakan Sevimli; Ayse Carlioglu; Pinar Mazlum Macit
medicalEvidence.summary: Reported a fibromyalgia prevalence of approximately 30 to 40 percent in patients with Hashimoto thyroiditis with structural pathology compared with roughly 2 to 7 percent in the general population, and described a relationship with thyroid disease activity — the primary prevalence evidence linking thyroid autoimmunity to fibromyalgia.

medicalEvidence.title: Is thyroid autoimmunity a predisposing factor for fibromyalgia? A systematic review and meta-analysis
medicalEvidence.authors: Seoeun Park; Jeong-Seung Kwon; Yong-Beom Park; Ji Woon Park
medicalEvidence.summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis concluding that autoimmune thyroid disease and elevated thyroid autoantibodies are associated with fibromyalgia and widespread chronic pain, with correlated clinical symptoms and depression — pooled evidence for the endocrine-to-central-pain pathway.

medicalEvidence.title: High prevalence of anti-TSH receptor antibody in fibromyalgia syndrome
medicalEvidence.authors: Kenya Nishioka; Toyoyoshi Uchida; Chie Usui; Ryota Tanaka; Takashi Matsushima; Yoshifuji Matsumoto; Ikuro Nakamura; Kusuki Nishioka; Nobutaka Hattori
medicalEvidence.summary: In 207 patients with clinically defined fibromyalgia syndrome, thyroid function testing and antibody assays found a high prevalence of anti-thyroid-stimulating-hormone-receptor antibody, especially prominent in that population — direct human evidence of a substantial thyroid-autoimmune overlap in fibromyalgia.

secondaryCondition: Meniere's disease (secondary endolymphatic hydrops) following service-connected traumatic brain injury residuals
secondaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.87, DC 6205 (Meniere's syndrome (endolymphatic hydrops)): 100 percent for hearing impairment with attacks of vertigo and cerebellar gait occurring more than once weekly; 60 percent for one to four attacks a month; 30 percent for vertigo less than once a month; with the note that the condition may instead be evaluated by separately rating vertigo as a peripheral vestibular disorder (DC 6204), hearing impairment, and tinnitus (DC 6260), whichever method yields the higher overall evaluation, but with no combining of those separate evaluations with an evaluation under DC 6205. Qualified-human rating review required
primaryCondition: Service-connected residuals of traumatic brain injury, with a documented closed-head or blast injury and persistent physical residuals including balance or vestibular dysfunction
primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.124a, DC 8045 (residuals of traumatic brain injury) — evaluated on the cognitive-impairment and subjective-symptoms table with separate evaluation of physical dysfunction under the appropriate diagnostic code; DC 8045 expressly directs that any residual with a distinct diagnosis that may be evaluated under another diagnostic code, such as migraine headache or Meniere's disease, be evaluated separately rather than under the table
etiologicalMechanism: Post-traumatic inner-ear fluid-homeostasis sequence: a blow to the head or a blast overpressure event delivers shearing and hydraulic force to the labyrinth, to the temporal bone, and to the endolymphatic sac and duct. Mechanical disruption of the membranous labyrinth allows potassium-rich endolymph to contaminate perilymph, depolarizing hair cells and producing episodic vertigo; injury or obstruction of the endolymphatic duct and sac impairs longitudinal flow and resorption of endolymph, so endolymphatic volume rises and secondary endolymphatic hydrops develops with fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and recurrent vertigo — the clinical profile of Meniere's disease. Ferster et al. (PMID 28306649) review secondary endolymphatic hydrops and identify it as a pathologic finding of the inner ear producing episodic vertigo and intermittent hearing loss, with post-mortem temporal-bone histopathology demonstrating hydrops in a post-traumatic case. Chung et al. (PMID 24782951) report a case of post-traumatic Meniere's disease in which the patient developed tinnitus, fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss, and recurrent vertigo, with symptom improvement only after endolymphatic sac decompression surgery, documenting a trauma-triggered hydrops that behaved as Meniere's disease. DiBiase and Arriaga (PMID 9386247) state that post-traumatic Meniere's disease is a true clinical entity based on clinical observation and histopathologic study, and that the traumatic insult may be a blow to the head or a temporal bone fracture, while they also record that many cases of Meniere's disease have no identifiable etiologic agent — an important limitation that the individual nexus opinion must confront rather than ignore. Framing under 38 CFR § 3.310: this is a § 3.310(a) direct-causation theory, in which the service-connected traumatic brain injury residuals are asserted to have caused a distinct inner-ear disease rated separately under DC 6205. It is not a § 3.310(b) aggravation theory; aggravation would be the correct theory only where the record shows idiopathic Meniere's disease or pre-existing vestibular disease before the head injury and the claim is that the trauma measurably worsened a baseline disorder, in which case the trauma-attributable increment must be separated from the natural progression of the pre-existing disease and § 3.310(b) governs. Chronology and the corresponding individual analysis require documentation that the head injury preceded the onset of the vertiginous and fluctuating hearing symptoms, that vestibular and audiologic testing supports endolymphatic hydrops (for example, fluctuating low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss with episodic vertigo), and that the examiner can state that the Meniere's disease is at least as likely as not caused by the service-connected traumatic brain injury — an opinion that requires a documented temporal sequence, an accounting for competing causes, and an approximate balance of evidence consistent with § 3.102. Competing causes that must be excluded or weighed include idiopathic Meniere's disease without any traumatic trigger, viral labyrinthitis, vestibular neuritis, otosclerosis, autoimmune inner ear disease, syphilis, noise-induced cochlear injury, benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, migraine-associated vertigo, and acoustic trauma, together with a positive family history of Meniere's disease; the discrimination is clinically demanding because most head injuries do not cause hydrops and because Meniere's disease is itself usually idiopathic. No individual probability is asserted here. Two rating cautions apply. First, DC 8045 itself forbids rating the same manifestation twice: vertigo, tinnitus, and hearing loss routed to DC 6205 may not simultaneously be used in the traumatic-brain-injury subjective-symptoms facet, consistent with § 4.14 non-pyramiding. Second, the note to DC 6205 bars combining an evaluation under DC 6205 with separate evaluations of hearing impairment, tinnitus, or vertigo, so only one coherent rating construct may be used.

medicalEvidence.title: Secondary Endolymphatic Hydrops
medicalEvidence.authors: Ashley P O'Connell Ferster; Sebahattin Cureoglu; Nevra Keskin; Michael M Paparella; Huseyin Isildak
medicalEvidence.summary: Review establishing secondary endolymphatic hydrops as an inner-ear pathologic finding that produces episodic vertigo and intermittent hearing loss, with post-mortem temporal-bone histopathology demonstrating hydrops plus necrotic organ of Corti in a post-traumatic case — the mechanistic source linking head trauma to hydrops.

medicalEvidence.title: A Case of Post-Traumatic Meniere's Disease
medicalEvidence.authors: Juyong Chung; Hahn Jin Jung; Chong Sun Kim; Young Ho Kim
medicalEvidence.summary: Case report of post-traumatic Meniere's disease following head trauma, with tinnitus, fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss, and recurrent vertigo that failed symptomatic medical treatment and improved markedly only after endolymphatic sac decompression — documented human example of the trauma-to-Meniere's sequence.

medicalEvidence.title: Post-traumatic hydrops
medicalEvidence.summary: Clinical and histopathologic analysis stating that post-traumatic Meniere's disease is a true clinical entity, that the traumatic insult may be a blow to the head or a temporal bone fracture, and simultaneously recording that many Meniere's disease cases have no identifiable etiologic agent — the etiologic-affirmation evidence together with its candid limitation.

secondaryCondition: Dry eye syndrome (keratoconjunctivitis sicca and thyroid-eye-disease-associated ocular surface disease) in a veteran with service-connected hyperthyroidism
secondaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.79, DC 6025 (disorders of the lacrimal apparatus (epiphora, dacryocystitis, etc.)): 20 percent bilateral and 10 percent unilateral; where punctate corneal epithelial disease is documented, DC 6001 (keratopathy) is also available and is evaluated under the General Rating Formula for Diseases of the Eye, subject to the prohibition on pyramiding the same visual impairment under § 4.14. Qualified-human rating review required; a clinically justified analogous evaluation under §§ 4.20 and 4.27 may be required where the predominant disability picture is tear-film failure without a lacrimal-apparatus diagnosis
primaryCondition: Service-connected hyperthyroidism, including Graves' disease, with documented thyroid-stimulating-hormone-receptor antibody positivity or clinical thyrotoxicosis
primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.119, DC 7900 (hyperthyroidism, including, but not limited to, Graves' disease): 30 percent for six months after initial diagnosis, with residuals of disease or complications of medical treatment thereafter rated within the appropriate diagnostic code in the appropriate body system; Note (2) expressly directs that eye involvement occurring as a manifestation of Graves' disease be separately evaluated as diplopia (DC 6090), impairment of central visual acuity (DCs 6061 through 6066), or under the most appropriate diagnostic codes in § 4.79
etiologicalMechanism: Orbitopathy and tear-film sequence: in service-connected hyperthyroidism due to Graves' disease, thyroid-stimulating-hormone-receptor autoantibodies activate orbital fibroblasts, driving glycosaminoglycan and hyaluronan deposition, adipogenesis, and cytokine-mediated orbital inflammation. The resulting proptosis, eyelid retraction, restrictive myopathy, and widened palpebral fissure increase the exposed ocular surface area and reduce the completeness of eyelid closure, so the tear film destabilizes and evaporates faster than the lacrimal system can replace it; lymphocytic infiltration and dysfunction of the lacrimal and accessory glands further reduce aqueous secretion, and the consequent ocular surface inflammation perpetuates tear-film instability and punctate epithelial damage. Selter et al. (PMID 25584018) reviewed the relationship between Graves' ophthalmopathy and dry eye syndrome and concluded that an increased risk of dry eye syndrome exists in patients with thyroid disease, describing a complex and bidirectional clinical relationship. Rana et al. (PMID 35167950) reviewed ocular surface disease in thyroid eye disease and reported that the prevalence of ocular surface disease among thyroid eye disease patients is estimated to range from about 65 to 95 percent, and that ocular surface inflammation and multifactorial changes to ocular surface homeostasis contribute substantially alongside the anatomical proptosis and corneal exposure mechanism. McAlinden (PMID 26605355) provides the epidemiologic linkage in his overview of thyroid eye disease, reporting that approximately 60 percent of patients with hyperthyroidism develop thyroid eye disease and that among thyroid eye disease patients roughly 85 percent are hyperthyroid, 10 percent hypothyroid, and 5 percent euthyroid — the last figure being the critical limitation for this theory. Framing under 38 CFR § 3.310: this is a § 3.310(a) direct-causation theory, in which the service-connected hyperthyroidism is asserted to have caused dry eye syndrome as an orbital and ocular-surface manifestation of the same autoimmune process. It is not a § 3.310(b) aggravation theory; aggravation would be the correct theory only where the record documents dry eye syndrome predating the thyroid disease and the claim is that the thyroid orbitopathy worsened a baseline tear-film disorder, in which case the attributable increment must be separated from the natural progression of that baseline condition and § 3.310(b) governs. Chronology and the individual analysis under § 3.310(a) or (b) require that the hyperthyroidism or Graves' disease diagnosis, and ideally thyroid-stimulating-hormone-receptor antibody status, precede or coincide with the onset of dry eye symptoms and objective ocular surface signs such as reduced tear break-up time, positive ocular surface staining, or Schirmer testing, so that the examiner can state that the dry eye syndrome is at least as likely as not caused by the service-connected hyperthyroidism — an opinion requiring a documented temporal sequence, an accounting for competing causes, and an approximate balance of evidence consistent with § 3.102. Competing causes that must be weighed include age-related tear deficiency, meibomian gland dysfunction and blepharitis, contact-lens wear, environmental exposure and screen-related tear evaporation, systemic medications such as antihistamines, tricyclic antidepressants, and isotretinoin, Sjögren's syndrome and other autoimmune sicca disease, diabetes mellitus, and prior ocular surgery or radiation. A further individualized caution: because thyroid eye disease and dry eye can occur in euthyroid and hypothyroid patients, the presence of dry eye in a veteran with treated thyroid disease does not by itself establish causation, and the nexus opinion must tie the ocular surface disease to the Graves' autoimmune process rather than to thyroid hormone levels alone. No individual probability is asserted here. Rating discipline under § 4.14: where dry eye has produced visual impairment that is separately rated under DCs 6061 through 6066 or under another § 4.79 code, the same impairment may not be rated a second time, and DC 7900 Note (2) and DC 7903 Note (3) both contemplate a single coordinate evaluation under § 4.79 for the eye involvement.

medicalEvidence.title: The relationship between Graves' ophthalmopathy and dry eye syndrome
medicalEvidence.authors: Jessica H Selter; Anisa I Gire; Shameema Sikder
medicalEvidence.summary: Literature review concluding that a complex relationship exists between Graves' ophthalmopathy and dry eye syndrome and that patients with thyroid disease carry an increased risk of dry eye syndrome — direct human evidence of the thyroid-eye-to-ocular-surface pathway.

medicalEvidence.title: Ocular Surface Disease in Thyroid Eye Disease: A Narrative Review
medicalEvidence.authors: Harkaran S Rana; Sruti S Akella; Carson E Clabeaux; Zachary P Skurski; Vinay K Aakalu
medicalEvidence.summary: Narrative review reporting that the prevalence of ocular surface disease among thyroid eye disease patients is estimated at roughly 65 to 95 percent, and that ocular surface inflammation and multifactorial disruption of ocular surface homeostasis contribute substantially alongside proptosis and corneal exposure — the quantitative and mechanistic link.

medicalEvidence.title: An overview of thyroid eye disease
medicalEvidence.summary: Overview of thyroid eye disease epidemiology, risk factors, and pathogenesis reporting that approximately 60 percent of patients with hyperthyroidism develop thyroid eye disease and that among thyroid eye disease patients about 85 percent are hyperthyroid, 10 percent hypothyroid, and 5 percent euthyroid — the epidemiologic linkage together with its individualized limitation.

secondaryCondition: Meralgia paresthetica (lateral femoral cutaneous neuropathy with painful anterolateral thigh dysesthesia) in a veteran with service-connected type 2 diabetes mellitus
secondaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.124a, DC 8529 (external cutaneous nerve of thigh): 10 percent for severe to complete paralysis, 0 percent for mild or moderate paralysis; where the presentation is inflammatory rather than paralytic, the corresponding neuritis code DC 8629 (external cutaneous nerve of thigh neuritis) applies, and where the presentation is purely sensory pain, DC 8729 (neuralgia) applies. Qualified-human rating review required — the maximum 10 percent evaluation under DC 8529 means the benefit of this mapping is frequently a 10 percent rating plus establishment of secondary service connection
primaryCondition: Service-connected type 2 diabetes mellitus, with documented diagnostic laboratory criteria and duration of disease
primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.119, DC 7913 (diabetes mellitus), assigned on the insulin, dietary, activity-regulation, and complication tiers, including the 20 percent tier for diabetes managed by regulation of diet or oral medication, with the note to DC 7913 addressing the relationship between diabetes and its separately evaluated complications
etiologicalMechanism: Metabolic-and-entrapment sequence: in service-connected type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic hyperglycemia drives nerve injury through polyol-pathway flux with sorbitol accumulation, formation of advanced glycation end products, oxidative stress, and impairment of the endoneurial microvasculature, so axons become more susceptible to mechanical deformation. The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve is anatomically vulnerable where it angulates as it passes beneath or through the inguinal ligament, and in the diabetic phenotype co-existing central adiposity and increased intra-abdominal pressure add extrinsic compression and further elevate intraneural pressure at that site. The combination converts a tolerable anatomic narrowing into a symptomatic mononeuropathy, producing burning, numbness, and painful dysesthesia over the anterolateral thigh that spare strength and deep tendon reflexes. Parisi et al. (PMID 21975198) conducted a population-based study in Olmsted County, Minnesota, identifying 262 patients with meralgia paresthetica against 262 normal controls and concluded that diabetes mellitus appears to be an independent risk factor for the development of meralgia paresthetica, while also recording the important observation that patients who have both meralgia paresthetica and diabetes mellitus tend to develop meralgia paresthetica before the diabetes is diagnosed. Weng et al. (PMID 28511974) analyzed etiologies in a hospital-based referral series of patients with electrodiagnostically confirmed meralgia paresthetica in Taiwan and found that obesity and certain occupations carried increased risk while only a small minority (approximately 2 percent) of their cases had diabetes mellitus, which is a direct internal counterweight to the diabetes-specific theory and must be disclosed. Chalk and Namiranian (PMID 38697741) review meralgia paresthetica and list diabetes mellitus among the recognized risk factors along with obesity, tight clothing, and prior hip or lumbar spine surgery. Framing under 38 CFR § 3.310: this is a § 3.310(a) direct-causation theory, in which the service-connected type 2 diabetes mellitus is asserted to have caused a new mononeuropathy affecting the external cutaneous nerve of the thigh. It is not a § 3.310(b) aggravation theory; aggravation would be the correct theory only where the record documents meralgia paresthetica predating the diabetes and the claim is that the metabolic disease worsened a baseline entrapment neuropathy, in which case the diabetes-attributable increment must be separated from the natural progression of a pre-existing compression neuropathy and § 3.310(b) governs. Chronology and the individual analysis under § 3.310(a) or (b) require a documented diagnosis of type 2 diabetes with its laboratory confirmation, documentation of meralgia paresthetica by clinical description and ideally by sensory nerve conduction study or somatosensory evoked potentials with normal strength and reflexes, and a temporal sequence in which the diabetic metabolic derangement precedes or coincides with the onset of the thigh dysesthesia, so that the examiner can state that the meralgia paresthetica is at least as likely as not caused by the service-connected diabetes — a conclusion requiring documented chronology, accounted-for competing causes, and an approximate balance of evidence, consistent with § 3.102. A specific evidentiary caution follows from the Parisi finding that meralgia paresthetica often precedes the clinical diagnosis of diabetes: in such cases the examiner must address whether undiagnosed glucose intolerance was already operative, or the nexus opinion should be framed as aggravation or left unestablished. Competing causes that must be excluded or weighed include obesity and rapid weight change, tight belts, garments, or body armor, prolonged sitting or standing postures with hip flexion, pregnancy, prior hip or lumbosacral spine surgery or iliac crest bone graft harvest, direct groin trauma, pelvic tumors or retroperitoneal mass, lead toxicity, hypothyroidism, and other metabolic neuropathies. No individual probability is asserted here. Rating discipline under § 4.14: sensory loss and pain in the anterolateral thigh may be rated only once — DC 8529, DC 8629, or DC 8729 — and the same sensory deficit may not simultaneously support an evaluation of diabetic peripheral neuropathy on the same extremity, consistent with § 4.14 non-pyramiding and with the note to DC 7913 requiring complications to be evaluated under the appropriate diagnostic code.

medicalEvidence.title: Meralgia paresthetica: relation to obesity, advanced age, and diabetes mellitus
medicalEvidence.authors: Thomas J Parisi; Jay Mandrekar; P James B Dyck; Christopher J Klein
medicalEvidence.summary: Population-based study in Olmsted County, Minnesota, identifying 262 patients with meralgia paresthetica and 262 normal controls, concluding that diabetes mellitus appears to be an independent risk factor for meralgia paresthetica while also noting that patients with both conditions often develop the neuropathy before the diabetes is diagnosed — the primary diabetes-to-neuropathy evidence and its caveat.

medicalEvidence.title: Risk factor analysis for meralgia paresthetica: A hospital-based study in Taiwan
medicalEvidence.authors: Wei-Chieh Weng; Yi-Chia Wei; Wen-Yi Huang; Yu-Yi Chien; Tsung-I Peng; Chia-Lun Wu
medicalEvidence.summary: Retrospective etiologic analysis of electromyographically confirmed meralgia paresthetica referral patients finding that male middle-aged patients with higher body mass index and certain occupations were at increased risk while only a small minority (about 2 percent) had diabetes mellitus — the counterweight showing that diabetes is neither necessary nor sufficient for this neuropathy.

medicalEvidence.title: Meralgia paresthetica
medicalEvidence.summary: Clinical review of meralgia paresthetica describing its diagnosis by history of painful sensory disturbance on the anterolateral thigh with normal strength and reflexes, and listing obesity, tight clothing, and diabetes mellitus among its risk factors — the diagnostic-criteria and risk-factor source for the mapping.

cfrCitations: 38 CFR § 4.124a, DC 8529 (external cutaneous nerve of thigh), DC 8629 (neuritis), and DC 8729 (neuralgia)
